<reason>B had the sharper mid-debate rebuttals (the "choose one" tension, the scarcity-rent dilemma, and the best single answer of the round in B4.1's observable-conduct distinction), and A lost some of its toolkit answer to a clipped rebuttal. But B's route degraded late: B conceded the destination (conversion of primary forest/peat should stop), shifting to "our instruments instead," yet its toolkit never closed the legal conversion channel — conduct law punishes illegal acts, buyer conditions leave residual discounted buyers, and mapping-first delays closure under harms A established as irreversible. A's closing permit/sequencing point ("they do not retire the permit that makes clearing official"; "sequence after the line, not instead of it") went unanswered despite B having the final word. Meanwhile B's distribution attack largely re-invoiced costs the motion explicitly stipulates, and the scarcity-rent dilemma was overclaimed (B never showed displacement would exceed the conversion prevented; A's channel-cost mechanism was at least as plausible). A's path — irreversible public losses versus stipulated reversible costs, with the legal channel closed now — survived cleaner.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The strongest exchange ran from A's Q1 (why would a captured state obey CON's existing law?) to B4.1's reply that fire/concession law punishes observable conduct without manufacturing a scarcity rent — the debate's sharpest single answer. But the decisive move was A's unanswered closing crystallization that CON's sequence keeps the frontier legally convertible while mapping and payments catch up, which under irreversible loss is "the land race with better manners."</best_rebuttal>
